# m07-l01 narration (generated from the outline; do not edit)

## Slide 1

Early Observations.

Copernicus showed that planetary motion is much easier to understand if Earth and the other planets revolve around the Sun.

Our big question for this lesson: what role does gravity play in planetary motion? To answer it, we'll start long before anyone knew what gravity was.

In ancient times, people assumed the Sun, the Moon, the planets, and the stars all circled Earth. But the Polish astronomer Nicholas Copernicus noticed that the planets' movements didn't fully fit that Earth-centered picture. His life's work, published in 1543 while he lay on his deathbed, showed that the motion of the planets makes much more sense if Earth and the other planets revolve around the Sun. His model even explained why Mercury and Venus, the inner planets, always appear near the Sun in our sky.

## Slide 2

Tycho Brahe's Measurements.

Tycho Brahe made the most accurate naked-eye measurements of planetary positions of his time.

Tycho Brahe was born a few years after Copernicus died. He realized the star charts of his day did a poor job of predicting astronomical events, and he knew the fix was careful measurements taken from one spot over a long stretch of time.

Tycho was given an estate on the Danish island of Hven, plus the money to build an early research institute. Telescopes hadn't been invented yet, so he designed and built giant measuring instruments in his own workshop, like the ones in Figure 1. With them he made the most accurate measurements of his time.

## Slide 4

Kepler's First Law.

Kepler's first law: the paths of the planets are ellipses, with the Sun at one focus.

In 1599, Tycho moved to Prague, and in 1600 a 28-year-old German named Johannes Kepler became one of his assistants. After Tycho died in 1601, Kepler kept studying his data, using geometry and mathematics to explain how the planets move. After seven years of careful work on Tycho's measurements of Mars, Kepler discovered laws that describe the motion of every planet and satellite, natural or artificial.

Kepler's first law says the paths of the planets are ellipses, with the Sun at one focus. An ellipse has two foci, as Figure 2 shows. So what's the common feature of every orbit around the Sun? Each one is an ellipse with the Sun sitting at one focus. The diagrams stretch the ellipses to make them easy to see, but Earth's real orbit is so close to a circle that you couldn't tell the difference by eye.

## Slide 5

Kepler's Second Law.

Kepler's second law: a line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals.

Kepler noticed that orbits can change because of gravitational effects from, or collisions with, other objects in the solar system. He also found that planets move faster when they're closer to the Sun and slower when they're farther away.

Kepler's second law says an imaginary line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals, as Figure 3 shows. Why are the equal areas shaped differently? Near the Sun, the line is short, so the planet has to cover a lot of its orbit, moving fast, to sweep out its share of area, making a short, wide wedge. Far from the Sun, the line is long, so a small slice of orbit is enough, making a long, skinny wedge.

## Slide 6

Kepler's Third Law.

Kepler's third law: the square of the ratio of two planets' periods equals the cube of the ratio of their average distances from the Sun.

A period is the time it takes an orbiting body to make one revolution. Kepler also found a mathematical link between the periods of the planets and their average distances from the Sun.

Kepler's third law says the square of the ratio of the periods of any two planets orbiting the Sun equals the cube of the ratio of their average distances from the Sun. In symbols: the square of T sub A over T sub B equals the cube of r sub A over r sub B, where T is a period and r is the distance from the center of the planet to the center of the Sun.

Here's a key difference. Kepler's first two laws apply to each planet, moon, or satellite on its own. The third law compares two objects orbiting the same central body. You can use it with the planets' distances from the Sun in Table 1, or to compare the Moon and artificial satellites orbiting Earth.

## Slide 7

Comet Periods.

Long-period comets take more than 200 years to orbit the Sun; short-period comets take less than 200 years.

Comets are sorted by their orbital periods. Long-period comets take more than 200 years to go around the Sun, and short-period comets take less than 200 years.

Comet McNaught, also called C slash 2006 P1, shown in Figure 4, has a period of about 92,000 years, so it's a long-period comet. Comet Halley comes around every 76 years, so it's a short-period comet. Comets obey Kepler's laws too, but unlike the planets, their orbits are highly elliptical.

## Slide 8

Example Problem 1, Callisto's Distance from Jupiter.

Solve Kepler's third law for the unknown radius: r sub C equals the cube root of the cube of r sub I times the square of T sub C over T sub I.

Galileo measured the orbits of Jupiter's moons using Jupiter's diameter as his unit. He found that Io, the closest moon, has a period of 1.8 days and orbits 4.2 units from Jupiter's center. Callisto, the fourth moon out, has a period of 16.7 days. Using Galileo's units, predict Callisto's distance from Jupiter.

Step one: analyze and sketch. Sketch the orbits of Io and Callisto and label their radii. Known: T sub C is 16.7 days, T sub I is 1.8 days, and r sub I is 4.2 units. Unknown: r sub C.

Step two: solve. Start with Kepler's third law: the square of T sub C over T sub I equals the cube of r sub C over r sub I. Rearranging, the cube of r sub C equals the cube of r sub I times the square of T sub C over T sub I. Take the cube root of both sides. Substitute 4.2 units for r sub I, 16.7 days for T sub C, and 1.8 days for T sub I. The quantity inside the cube root works out to 6.4 times 10 to the third cubic units, and its cube root is 19 units.

Step three: evaluate. Are the units right? Yes, r sub C comes out in Galileo's units, just like r sub I. Is the size realistic? Callisto's period is longer, so its orbit should be bigger, and it is.

## Slide 9

Newton's Inverse Square Insight.

The gravitational force between two objects is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers.

In 1666, Isaac Newton began studying planetary motion. The story goes that watching an apple fall made him wonder whether the force pulling the apple down might reach all the way to the Moon, or even farther.

He found that the size of the force F sub g on a planet due to the Sun varies inversely with the square of the distance r between their centers. In other words, F sub g is proportional to one over the square of r. The force points along the line joining the two centers, as Figure 5 shows. Newton found that the accelerations of both the apple and the Moon fit this one over the square of r relationship.

By his own third law, the force Earth exerts on the apple is exactly equal in size to the force the apple exerts on Earth. So why do we only see the apple move? Because the apple has so much less mass than Earth. Newton reasoned that the attraction between two objects must be proportional to their masses. We call it the gravitational force.

## Slide 10

The Law of Universal Gravitation.

Every two objects attract with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers.

Newton was confident that the same attraction acts between any two objects anywhere in the universe. His law of universal gravitation says that objects attract each other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

As an equation: F sub g equals capital G times m sub 1 times m sub 2, divided by the square of r. Here F sub g is the gravitational force, capital G is the universal gravitational constant, m sub 1 and m sub 2 are the two masses, and r is the distance between their centers.

Since F sub g is directly proportional to each mass, doubling the mass of a planet near the Sun doubles the force of attraction. Figure 6 shows the inverse square part as a graph: the force drops steeply as the distance grows.

## Slide 11

Connecting Math to Physics, Direct and Inverse Relationships.

F sub g is proportional to m sub 1 times m sub 2 and proportional to one over the square of r.

Newton's law mixes a direct relationship and an inverse one. Let's play with them. If you double one mass, the force doubles. Triple one mass, and the force triples. Double one mass and triple the other, and the force becomes six times as big. Cut both masses in half, and the force drops to one fourth.

Distance works the other way, and it works through the square. Double the distance, and the force drops to one fourth. Triple the distance, and the force drops to one ninth. Cut the distance in half, and the force becomes four times as big. Cut it to a third, and the force becomes nine times as big.

## Slide 12

Universal Gravitation and Kepler's Third Law.

For a circular orbit, setting gravity equal to the planet's mass times its centripetal acceleration gives: the square of T equals four pi squared over G m sub s, times the cube of r.

Newton stated his law in a way that fit the motion of the planets around the Sun, and it agreed with Kepler's third law. That told him his law matched the best observations of the day.

Picture a planet orbiting the Sun, as in Figure 7. Newton's second law says F sub net equals m sub p times a sub c, where m sub p is the planet's mass and a sub c is its centripetal acceleration. To keep things simple, assume a circular orbit. From circular motion, a sub c equals 4 times the square of pi times r, divided by the square of T, where T is the time in seconds for one full trip around the Sun. So the net force is m sub p times 4 times the square of pi times r, divided by the square of T.

The net force here is gravity. Set that expression equal to capital G times m sub s times m sub p over the square of r, where m sub s is the Sun's mass. The planet's mass cancels, and rearranging gives: the square of T equals 4 times the square of pi, divided by capital G times m sub s, all times the cube of r. Taking the square root, T equals 2 pi times the square root of the cube of r divided by capital G times m sub s.

So how does gravity explain a planet's orbit? The Sun's gravitational pull is the centripetal force that keeps bending the planet's path into a closed orbit instead of letting it fly off in a straight line.

## Slide 13

The Period of a Planet.

T equals 2 pi times the square root of the cube of r divided by G m sub s.

So the period of a planet orbiting the Sun is 2 pi times the square root of the cube of its average distance from the Sun, divided by the product of the universal gravitational constant and the Sun's mass.

Square both sides and you get Kepler's third law back: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the distance between the masses. The factor 4 times the square of pi over capital G m sub s depends only on the Sun's mass and the universal gravitational constant, so it's the same for every planet. Newton found that this factor works for elliptical orbits too.

## Slide 14

Measuring the Universal Gravitational Constant.

Henry Cavendish measured G in 1798 using a sensitive torsion balance.

How big is capital G? The gravitational pull between ordinary objects on Earth is tiny. Even two massive bowling balls attract each other so weakly that the force is nearly impossible to detect. It took about 100 years after Newton's work for scientists to build an apparatus sensitive enough to measure it.

In 1798, the English scientist Henry Cavendish used equipment like the apparatus in Figure 8. A horizontal rod with a small lead sphere on each end hangs from its midpoint by a thin wire, so it can twist. Because the wire is so thin, the rod responds to even very small horizontal forces.

Two large spheres are fixed close to the two small spheres. Their attraction makes the rod twist until the wire's twisting force balances the gravitational force, and then the rod stops. A beam of light reflecting off a mirror on the wire measures the angle of twist, which gives the force. With the force, the masses, and the distances between centers all known, Newton's law gives capital G: 6.67 times 10 to the negative 11 newton meters squared per kilogram squared.

## Slide 15

Crosscutting Concepts, Patterns.

Patterns observed in a small laboratory experiment can explain phenomena on the scale of the solar system.

Here's a crosscutting idea worth chewing on: patterns. Cavendish worked with lead spheres on a tabletop, yet the same law he tested describes moons, planets, and the Sun.

Your challenge: create a presentation that explains how the patterns Cavendish observed in his small-scale experiment give evidence that explains phenomena on a much larger scale, like the interactions within the solar system.

## Slide 16

The Importance of G.

Knowing G lets us calculate the gravitational force between any two objects and find the masses of Earth and the Sun.

Cavendish's experiment is often called weighing Earth, because once you know capital G, you can find the mass of Earth, and even of the Sun. You can also find the gravitational force between any two objects.

Try it with two bowling balls, each 7.26 kilograms, with centers 0.30 meters apart. F sub g equals 6.67 times 10 to the negative 11 newton meters squared per kilogram squared, times 7.26 kilograms, times 7.26 kilograms, divided by the square of 0.30 meters. That's 3.9 times 10 to the negative 8 newtons. Tiny!

Now the Earth. On Earth's surface, an object's weight is F sub g equals m g. Writing Earth's mass as m sub E and its radius as r sub E, gravity also says F sub g equals capital G m sub E m over the square of r sub E. So g equals capital G m sub E over the square of r sub E. Rearranged, m sub E equals g times the square of r sub E, divided by capital G. Using g equals 9.8 newtons per kilogram, r sub E equals 6.38 times 10 to the sixth meters, and capital G equals 6.67 times 10 to the negative 11 newton meters squared per kilogram squared, Earth's mass comes out to 5.98 times 10 to the 24th kilograms.

So Cavendish's work found capital G, confirmed Newton's prediction that every two objects attract, and helped calculate Earth's mass. And now our focus question has its answer: gravity is the force that holds planets in their orbits, and it's the very same force that makes an apple fall.
